subject: Energy
title: Nuclear Fuel Rods
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Nuclear Fuel Rods.

hook.text: Reactor fuel is packed into long, thin rods—uranium oxide pellets stacked inside metal tubes called cladding.

buildup.text: Each pellet is about 1 cm tall and holds as much energy as 800 kg of coal—the density is extraordinary.

discovery.text: Fuel rods are bundled into assemblies—a typical reactor contains hundreds of assemblies with millions of pellets.

twist.text: Fuel rods last 4–6 years before fission products accumulate and efficiency drops—then they must be replaced.

climax.text: Spent fuel remains intensely radioactive—and produces enough heat to require active cooling for years.

punchline.text: Tiny pellets, years of power—then decades of cooling.

quiz.question: How long do fuel rods typically last in a reactor?
